::: :::: ::: {.notes} Each of us give a brief intro on our experience/background ::: ## Prerequisites {.bkg-left} **Tidyverse familiarity** ::: {.incremental} - Selecting a set of variables (`select(starts_with("TOT"))`) - Creating new variables with `mutate()` - Summarizing data with `summarize()` - Using `group_by()` with `summarize()` to create group summaries ::: ## Overview of tutorial {.bkg-trees} At the end of this tutorial, you should be able to: ::: {.incremental} - Specify a survey design in R to create a survey object - Calculate point estimates and their standard errors with survey data - Create tables and graphs incorporating survey data and standard errors ::: ## Logistics {.bkg-right} - We will be using Posit Cloud for exercises - All materials are found at: - (Site) - (Source) ## Libraries Needed for Today {.bkg-ship} _Note: These are already installed in Posit Cloud_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(survey) library(srvyr) library(gt) library(sf) library(tmap) ``` ::: ## R Packages for Survey Analysis {.bkg-ship} ::::: {.columns} :::: {.column width=49%} ::: {.fragment} - {survey} package first on CRAN in 2003 - descriptive analysis - statistical testing - modeling - weighting ::: :::: ::: {.column width=2%} ::: ::: {.column width=49%} ::: {.fragment} - {srvyr} package first on CRAN in 2016 - “wrapper” for {survey} with {tidyverse}-style syntax - only descriptive analysis ::: :::: ::::: ## Why use {srvyr} over {survey}? ::: {.incremental} - Use the pipe function `%>%` or `|>` - Ability to use tidy selection - Functions follow `snake_case` convention ::: # Comparison of {dplyr} and {srvyr} Functions {background-color='{{< brand color blue >}}' .bkg-buildings} ## Apply {dplyr} functions to survey objects - A few functions in {srvyr} have counterparts in {dplyr} - `dplyr::summarize()` and `srvyr::summarize()` - `dplyr::group_by()` and `srvyr::group_by()` - Based on the object class, R will recognize which package to use ## Using `summarize()` to calculate mean and median ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Tibble: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|1|2,4|3|"} towny %>% summarize( area_mean = mean(land_area_km2, na.rm=TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 area_mean 1 373. ``` ::: ::: ### Survey object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anes_des %>% summarize( age_mean = survey_mean(Age, na.rm=TRUE), ) ``` ::: ::: ## Filtering and Selecting ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Tibble: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} towny %>% filter(csd_type == "township") %>% select(csd_type, name) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 195 × 2 csd_type name 1 township Addington Highlands 2 township Adelaide Metcalfe 3 township Adjala-Tosorontio 4 township Admaston/Bromley 5 township Alberton 6 township Alfred and Plantagenet 7 township Algonquin Highlands 8 township Alnwick/Haldimand 9 township Amaranth 10 township The Archipelago # ℹ 185 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Survey object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anes_des %>% filter(EducationGroup == "Graduate") %>% select(Sex) ``` ::: ::: ## Grouping ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Tibble: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} towny %>% group_by(csd_type) %>% summarize(area_mean = mean(land_area_km2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 csd_type area_mean 1 city 498. 2 municipality 607. 3 town 183. 4 township 363. 5 village 23.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Survey object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anes_des %>% group_by(EducationGroup) %>% summarize(age_mean = survey_mean(Age, na.rm=TRUE)) ``` ::: ::: ## Using {srvyr} functions on non-survey objects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} towny %>% summarize(area_mean = survey_mean(land_area_km2)) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `summarize()`: ℹ In argument: `area_mean = survey_mean(land_area_km2)`. Caused by error in `cur_svy()`: ! Survey context not set ``` ::: ::: # Introduction to the European Social Survey (ESS) ## Overview - Conducted across Europe every 2 years since 2001 - Cross-sectional sample (new samples each round) - Topics include living conditions, social structure, public opinion and attitudes - Sampling designs vary by country but have oversight for rigor ## Countries for round 11 (2023-2024) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/02-round-11-map-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Accessing ESS data 1. Create an account at the [ESS Data Portal](https://ess.sikt.no/en/register?redirectUrl=/en/) and then get your [user ID](https://ess.sikt.no/en/api) 2. Add your user ID to your R environ file by opening the file and editing as follows: ```r usethis::edit_r_environ() ``` Edit as follows (example): ```r ESS_USERID="12345678-1234-1234-1234-12345678900" ``` 3. Restart your R session 4. Load the ESS data into R ```r url <- glue::glue( "https://api.ess.sikt.no/v1/data/dataFile/10.21338/ess11e04_2?userId={Sys.getenv('ESS_USERID')}" ) ess_in <- read_parquet(url) ``` ## Read data subset for this course - This data is a subset of columns of full data - Includes derived variables we created for this course - See [data cleaning code](DataCleaning.qmd) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_der <- read_rds(here::here("DerivedData", "ess11_der.rds")) ``` ::: ## Why weight? Why use the design? - Differential selection probabilities and nonresponse are accounted for in analytic weights - Weights are post-stratified by gender, age, education, and geographic region - Not using weights leads to bias - Not using design likely leads to incorrect precision, wrong degrees of freedom and not accounting for clustering ## Estimates changing with weights ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/02-weight-compare-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## ESS Variable Viewer - Explore ESS variables at the [Variable Viewer](https://ess.sikt.no/en/datafile/242aaa39-3bbb-40f5-98bf-bfb1ce53d8ef?tab=1) --- format: revealjs --- # Setting up the design object # Sampling designs ## Sampling methods Units can be selected in various ways such as: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Simple random sampling** (with or without replacement) Every unit has the same chance of being selected ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Systematic sampling** Sample from an ordered list, selecting individuals at an interval with a random starting point ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Probability proportional to size** Probability of selection is proportional to "size" ::: ::: ## Complex designs Designs can also incorporate stratification and/or clustering: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Stratified sampling** Divide population into mutually exclusive subgroups (strata). Randomly sample within each stratum ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Clustered sampling** Divide population into mutually exclusive subgroups (clusters). Randomly sample clusters, then individuals within clusters ::: ::: ## Why does design matter? {.incremental} - The design type impacts the variability of the estimates - Weights impact the point estimate and the variability estimates - Specifying the components of the design (strata and/or clusters) and weights in R is necessary to get correct estimates ## Determining the design {.smaller} ::: {.incremental} - Check the documentation such as methodology, design, analysis guide, or technical documentation - Documentation will indicate the variables needed to specify the design. Look for: - **Weight** (almost always) - **Strata and/or clusters/PSUs** (sometimes labeled pseudo-strata/pseudo-clusters) — *or*, instead, **replicate weights** - **Finite population correction** or population sizes (uncommon) - Documentation may include SAS, SUDAAN, Stata and/or R syntax ::: ## Design-based vs. replicate weights Two ways to tell R about a sampling design, depending on what the documentation provides: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Strata / clusters / weights are available** Use `as_survey_design()` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Only replicate weights are available** Use `as_survey_rep()` ::: ::: - Some surveys provide both; others release only replicate weights to protect respondent confidentiality - Either path produces a `tbl_svy` object that works the same way downstream # Specifying sampling designs in {srvyr} **without** replicate weights ## `as_survey_design()`: Syntax - Specifying the sampling design when you don't have replicate weights - `as_survey_design()` creates a `tbl_svy` object that then correctly calculates weighted estimates and SEs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as_survey_design( .data, ids = NULL, # cluster IDs/PSUs strata = NULL, # strata variables variables = NULL, # defaults to all in .data fpc = NULL, # variables defining the fpc nest = FALSE, # TRUE/FALSE - relabel clusters to nest within strata check_strata = !nest, # check that clusters are nested in strata weights = NULL # weight variable, ) ``` ::: ## Syntax for common designs: no stratification/clustering {.smaller} Load in the example data from {survey} package: ```r data(api, package="survey") ``` . . . Simple Random Sample (SRS) ```r apisrs %>% as_survey_design(fpc = fpc) ``` . . . One-stage cluster sample with a FPC variable ```r apiclus1 %>% as_survey_design(ids = dnum, weights = pw, fpc = fpc) ``` . . . Two-stage cluster sample, weights computed from population size ```r apiclus2 %>% as_survey_design(ids = c(dnum, snum), fpc = c(fpc1, fpc2)) ``` ::: aside Examples from `srvyr` help documentation ::: ## Syntax for common designs: with stratification {.smaller} Stratified SRS ```r apistrat %>% as_survey_design(strata = stype, weights = pw) ``` . . . Stratified, cluster design ```r apistrat %>% as_survey_design(ids = dnum, strata = stype, weights = pw, nest = TRUE) ``` ::: aside Examples from `srvyr` help documentation ::: ## What does the design object look like? {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(api, package = "survey") apistrat_des <- apistrat |> select(cds, stype, api00, pw, fpc) |> as_survey_design(strata = stype, weights = pw) apistrat_des ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Stratified Independent Sampling design (with replacement) Called via srvyr Sampling variables: - ids: `1` - strata: stype - weights: pw Data variables: - cds (chr), stype (fct), api00 (int), pw (dbl), fpc (dbl) ``` ::: ::: ::: aside Data: `apistrat` from the `{survey}` package ::: # Replicate weight methods ## Replicate weights overview {.smaller} Replicate weights are another method to estimate variability. In general, they are constructed by: 1. Divide the sample into subsample replicates that mirror the design of the sample 2. Calculate weights for each replicate using the same procedures for the full-sample weight (i.e., nonresponse and post-stratification) 3. Calculate estimates for each replicate using the same method as the full-sample estimate 4. Calculate the estimated variance, which is proportional to the variance of the replicate estimates ## Common replicate weight methods - Balanced repeated replication (BRR) - Fay's BRR - Jackknife - Bootstrap # Specifying sampling designs in {srvyr} **with** replicate weights ## `as_survey_rep()`: Syntax {.smaller} - `as_survey_rep()` creates a `tbl_svy` object that then correctly calculates weighted estimates and SEs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as_survey_rep( .data, variables = NULL, # defaults to all in .data repweights = NULL, # Variables specifying the replication weights weights = NULL, # Variable specifying the analytic/main weight type = c( "BRR", "Fay", "JK1", "JKn", "bootstrap", "successive-difference", "ACS", "other" ), # Type of replication weight combined_weights = TRUE, # TRUE if repweights already include sampling weights, usually TRUE rho = NULL, # Shrinkage factor for Fay's method bootstrap_average = NULL, # For type="bootstrap", if the bootstrap weights have been averaged, gives the number of iterations averaged over scale = NULL, # Scaling constant for variance rscales = NULL, # Scaling constants for variance mse = getOption("survey.replicates.mse"), # If TRUE, compute variance based around point estimates rather than mean of replicates degf = NULL, # Design degrees of freedom, otherwise calculated based on number of replicate weights ) ``` ::: ## Worked example: BRR with real data {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(scd, package = "survey") scd <- scd |> mutate( rep1 = 2 * c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0), rep2 = 2 * c(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1), rep3 = 2 * c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1), rep4 = 2 * c(0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0) ) scd_rep <- scd |> as_survey_rep( type = "BRR", repweights = starts_with("rep"), combined_weights = FALSE ) scd_rep ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: Called via srvyr Balanced Repeated Replicates with 4 replicates. Sampling variables: - repweights: `rep1 + rep2 + rep3 + rep4` Data variables: - ESA (int), ambulance (int), arrests (dbl), alive (dbl), rep1 (dbl), rep2 (dbl), rep3 (dbl), rep4 (dbl) ``` ::: ::: ::: aside Data: `scd` from the `{survey}` package (Levy and Lemeshow BRR example) ::: ## Recap - Design type (SRS, stratified, clustered) shapes the variability of estimates - Weights shape both point estimates and variance - Two paths to a `tbl_svy` object: - `as_survey_design()`: strata, clusters/PSUs, weights - `as_survey_rep()`: replicate weights (BRR, Fay's, jackknife, bootstrap) - Once built, the design object is ready for weighted summaries in later sections # ESS sampling and weighting ## Methodology Recall, we said: "Check the documentation such as methodology, design, analysis guide, or technical documentation" Head to the ESS website and click "Methodology": ## Sampling {.smaller} Key sampling principles, from the ESS Sampling Guidelines: ::: {.incremental} - Samples represent all persons aged 15+ living in private households in each country - Individuals are selected by **strict random probability methods** at every stage — no quota sampling, no substitution of non-responders - Each country targets a minimum "effective achieved sample size" (1,500, or 800 in countries with populations under 2 million) - Exact designs (single-stage, stratified, multi-stage/clustered) **vary by country**, but every country's data include `psu` (primary sampling unit) and `stratum` variables ::: ::: aside ::: ## Weighting {.smaller} > Four weighting variables are available: Analysis weight (anweight - combination of pspwght and pweight), Post-stratification weight (pspwght), Design weight (dweight), and Population weight (pweight). ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **dweight** — corrects for unequal selection probabilities *within* a country **pspwght** — further adjusts `dweight` for nonresponse/noncoverage using age, gender, education, region ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **pweight** — rescales each country to its population size, for combining countries in one analysis **anweight** — `dweight` + `pspwght` + `pweight` combined; **recommended for all analyses** ::: ::: ::: aside ::: ## Weighting: the provided code {.smaller} Clicking into the "weighting guide," we find example R code using `anweight`, the recommended weight: ```r library(survey) # estimation # Define sample design design <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~anweight, data = data1) ``` ## First attempt Using exactly the syntax from the weighting guide, we get an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svydesign( ids = ~ psu, strata = ~ stratum, weights = ~ anweight, data = ess_der ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `svydesign.default()`: ! Clusters not nested in strata at top level; you may want nest=TRUE. ``` ::: ::: ## Why the error? {.smaller} A handful of `psu` codes repeat across different `stratum` values in the raw file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_der |> distinct(cntry, psu, stratum) |> add_count(psu) |> filter(n > 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 4 cntry psu stratum n 1 HU 12809 855 2 2 HU 13338 815 2 3 HU 13247 855 2 4 HU 13247 779 2 5 HU 12809 851 2 6 HU 13338 884 2 ``` ::: ::: By default, `svydesign()` assumes cluster (`psu`) IDs are unique across the whole data set. `nest = TRUE` tells it to relabel clusters so they're uniquely identified *within* each stratum instead — the same `nest` argument from the `as_survey_design()` syntax earlier ## Applying weights, fixed Including `nest = TRUE`, we get the design object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des_true <- svydesign( ids = ~ psu, strata = ~ stratum, weights = ~ anweight, data = ess_der, nest = TRUE ) ess_des_true ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement) With (24791) clusters. svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~anweight, data = ess_der, nest = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: ## From `{survey}` to `{srvyr}` The same design, specified with tidy syntax: ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des <- ess_der |> as_survey_design( ids = psu, strata = stratum, weights = anweight, nest = TRUE ) ess_des ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement) With (24791) clusters. Called via srvyr Sampling variables: - ids: psu - strata: stratum - weights: anweight Data variables: - cntry (chr), anweight (dbl), nwspol (int), netusoft (int), netustm (int), volunfp (int), happy (int), wrhpp (int), agegroup (int), pdwrk (int), edctn (int), uempla (int), uempli (int), dsbld (int), rtrd (int), cmsrv (int), hswrk (int), dngoth (int), dngref (int), dngdk (int), dngna (int), stratum (int), psu (int), pdwrk_rec (int), edctn_rec (int), uempla_rec (int), uempli_rec (int), dsbld_rec (int), rtrd_rec (int), cmsrv_rec (int), hswrk_rec (int), dngoth_rec (int), Retired (lgl), wt1 (dbl), Happy_Freq (int), Happy (int), News (int), Country (chr), Volunteer_12 (int), Volunteer_01 (dbl), Volunteer_Factor (fct), NetUsage (dbl), NetFreq (fct), AgeGroup (fct) ``` ::: ::: Same result: a `tbl_svy` object ready for weighted summaries. ## Back to design-based vs. replicate weights ESS falls on the **strata/clusters** side of that earlier choice: - The data provide `psu` and `stratum` variables (and a single analysis weight, `anweight`) — no replicate weights - That's why we used `as_survey_design()`/`svydesign()`, not `as_survey_rep()` - A survey that instead shipped jackknife or BRR replicate weights would call for `as_survey_rep()` the same way # Descriptive analysis ## Common workflow ::: incremental 1. Create a `tbl_svy` object (a survey object) using: `as_survey_design()` or `as_survey_rep()` 2. Subset data (if needed) using `filter()` (to create subpopulations) 3. Specify domains of analysis using `group_by()` 4. Within `summarize()`, specify variables to calculate, including means, totals, proportions, quantiles, and more ::: ## Descriptive functions {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Use within `summarize()` - `survey_mean(x)` - `survey_median(x)` - `survey_proportion()` - `survey_quantile(x)` - `survey_ratio(num, den)` - `survey_sd(x)` - `survey_total(x)` - `survey_var(x)` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Common arguments - `na.rm = FALSE` - `vartype = c("se", "ci", "var", "cv")`: defaults to just "se" - `level = 0.95`: confidence interval level of CIs - `deff = FALSE`: note can specify as logical OR "replace" - `df = NULL`: degrees of freedom for CIs (defaults to `degf(design)`) ::: :::: ::: {.notes} - survey_median/survey_quantile - no deff - survey_sd - no deff, no measures of variation - survey_var - no deff, no cv ::: ## Mean examples ::: {.panel-tabset} ### `na.rm` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "IS") |> summarize( H1 = survey_mean(News), H2 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 H1 H1_se H2 H2_se 1 NA NaN 56.9 3.27 ``` ::: ::: ### `vartype` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "IS") |> summarize( H1 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = c("se", "ci", "var", "cv")), H2 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = NULL) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 7 H1 H1_se H1_low H1_upp H1_var H1_cv H2 1 56.9 3.27 50.4 63.3 10.7 0.0575 56.9 ``` ::: ::: ### `level` and `df` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "IS") |> summarize( H1 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci", level = 0.95), H2 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci", level = 0.8), H3 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci", level = 0.95, df = 10) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 9 H1 H1_low H1_upp H2 H2_low H2_upp H3 H3_low H3_upp 1 56.9 50.4 63.3 56.9 52.7 61.1 56.9 49.6 64.1 ``` ::: ::: ### `deff` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "IS") |> summarize(H1 = survey_mean(News, na.rm = TRUE, deff = "replace")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 H1 H1_se H1_deff 1 56.9 3.27 1.39 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - na.rm removes NA before calculation, similar to many other functions in R - vartype can choose no option OR multiple - level and df control confidence intervals - deff is a design effect, a ratio of the variance under this design compared to a design which is SRS, >1 means less statistically efficient ::: ## Proportion example - motivation And still thinking about different ways of trying to improve things in [country] or help prevent things from going wrong, during the last 12 months, have you done any of the following? Have you volunteered for a not-for-profit or charitable organisation? (`volunfp`) - 1: yes - 2: no - 7: Refusal* - 8: Don't know* - 9: No answer* ## Proportion example - variable coding Derived variable coding options (unweighted raw data): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_der |> count( volunfp, Volunteer_12, Volunteer_01, Volunteer_Factor ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 volunfp Volunteer_12 Volunteer_01 Volunteer_Factor n 1 1 1 1 Yes 9305 2 2 2 0 No 40643 3 7 NA NA 92 4 8 NA NA 65 5 9 NA NA 11 ``` ::: ::: ## Proportion example - 2 ways Two methods for proportions 1. For binary outcomes, use `survey_mean(x)` - `x` is either 1/0 or TRUE/FALSE - can use with `across()` and several outcomes 2. Group the data by the variable (`x`) and then use `survey_prop()` - `x` can have 2 or more levels - only analyze one outcome at a time ::: aside See [Calculating estimates for many outcomes](https://tidy-survey-r.github.io/tidy-survey-book/c05-descriptive-analysis.html#calculating-estimates-for-many-outcomes) for extending to multiple outcomes ::: ## Proportion example - 2 ways ::: {.panel-tabset} ### `survey_mean()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "SE") |> summarize( across( c(Volunteer_12, Volunteer_01), ~ survey_mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 Volunteer_12 Volunteer_12_se Volunteer_01 Volunteer_01_se 1 1.74 0.0139 0.260 0.0139 ``` ::: ::: ### `survey_prop()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "SE", !is.na(Volunteer_Factor)) |> group_by(Volunteer_Factor) |> summarize(p = survey_prop()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 Volunteer_Factor p p_se 1 Yes 0.260 0.0139 2 No 0.740 0.0139 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - survey_mean method only works for binary outcomes, bonus of being able to use across to estimate many outcomes at once - survey_prop can be used for only one outcome at a time, can work for variables with more than 2 levels ::: ## Proportion example - arguments `proportion` argument in `survey_mean()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "SE") |> summarize( p1 = survey_mean(Volunteer_01, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci"), p2 = survey_mean( Volunteer_01, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci", proportion = TRUE ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 6 p1 p1_low p1_upp p2 p2_low p2_upp 1 0.260 0.232 0.287 0.260 0.233 0.288 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - proportion = TRUE argument only impacts confidence intervals ::: ## Proportion example - arguments `prop_method` argument in `survey_mean()/survey_prop()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "SE", !is.na(Volunteer_Factor)) |> group_by(Volunteer_Factor) |> summarize( p1 = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", prop_method = "logit"), p2 = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", prop_method = "mean"), p3 = survey_prop(vartype = "ci", prop_method = "xlogit") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 10 Volunteer_Factor p1 p1_low p1_upp p2 p2_low p2_upp p3 p3_low p3_upp 1 Yes 0.260 0.233 0.288 0.260 0.232 0.287 0.260 0.233 0.288 2 No 0.740 0.712 0.767 0.740 0.713 0.768 0.740 0.712 0.767 ``` ::: ::: ::: aside See [`?survey::svyciprop`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survey/refman/survey.html#svyciprop) for details on implementation ::: ## Subgroup analysis - Using `filter()` as above examples subsets data. This is done AFTER creating the design object - Use `group_by()` to implement domain analysis ## Subgroup analysis - mean and median - `NetUsage` is 0 if a person uses internet never, only occasionally, or a few times a week; otherwise the reported time of internet usage on a typical day (minutes) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ess_des |> group_by(Country) |> summarize( Pop = survey_total(vartype = NULL), NetUse_mean = survey_mean(NetUsage, na.rm = TRUE), NetUse_median = survey_median(NetUsage, na.rm = TRUE) ) |> gt() |> fmt_number(columns = starts_with("NetUse"), decimals = 2) |> fmt_number(columns = Pop, decimals = 0) |> opt_interactive(page_size_default = 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Subgroup analysis - proportion, marginal - `NetFreq` is how often people use the internet (categorical) - `AgeGroup` is a categorical age variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "FR", !is.na(NetFreq), !is.na(AgeGroup)) |> group_by(AgeGroup, NetFreq) |> summarize( N = survey_total() * 10000, p = survey_prop() * 100 ) |> gt() |> fmt_number(decimal = 1, columns = starts_with("p")) |> fmt_number(decimal = 0, columns = c(N, N_se)) |> opt_interactive(page_size_default = 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Subgroup analysis - proportion, joint ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ess_des |> filter(cntry == "FR", !is.na(NetFreq), !is.na(AgeGroup)) |> group_by(interact(AgeGroup, NetFreq)) |> summarize( N = survey_total() * 10000, p = survey_prop() * 100 ) |> gt() |> fmt_number(decimal = 1, columns = starts_with("p")) |> fmt_number(decimal = 0, columns = c(N, N_se)) |> opt_interactive(page_size_default = 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Visualizing survey estimates ## Map survey estimates - Country is a natural domain for ESS analysis - Choropleth maps make cross-country patterns easier to spot than a table - Builds on two earlier pieces: survey-weighted estimation (`srvyr`) + country shapes (`tmap`/`sf`) ## Step 1: estimate weighted mean happiness by country `Happy` is the ESS `happy` item (0 = extremely unhappy, 10 = extremely happy), with refusal/don't know/no answer codes already recoded to `NA`. We reuse `ess_des`, the design object built from `ess_der` in the ESS intro. ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} happy_by_country <- ess_des |> filter(!is.na(Happy)) |> group_by(Country) |> summarize(Happy_mean = survey_mean(Happy, na.rm = TRUE)) happy_by_country ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 30 × 3 Country Happy_mean Happy_mean_se 1 Austria 7.85 0.0494 2 Belgium 7.70 0.0464 3 Bulgaria 6.33 0.0549 4 Croatia 7.53 0.0569 5 Cyprus 6.99 0.0888 6 Estonia 7.31 0.0535 7 Finland 8.04 0.0427 8 France 7.43 0.0445 9 Germany 7.59 0.0675 10 Greece 6.80 0.0369 # ℹ 20 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: join estimates to country shapes Join on country name, then transform/crop to the same European extent used earlier. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} happy_shape <- World |> full_join(happy_by_country, by = c("name" = "Country")) |> st_transform(3035) |> st_crop( st_bbox(c(xmin = -10, ymin = 32, xmax = 36, ymax = 70), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(3035) ) ``` ::: ## Step 3: map colored by `Happy` ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} happy_shape |> tm_shape() + tm_polygons(fill = "lightgrey", col = "darkgrey") + tm_shape(happy_shape |> filter(!is.na(Happy_mean))) + tm_polygons( fill = "Happy_mean", fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues"), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Mean happiness\n(0-10 scale)") ) + tm_text("iso_a3") + tm_graticules() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/happy-map-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `tm_scale_continuous()` is used here (vs. `tm_scale_categorical()` in the earlier ESS-11 map) because `Happy_mean` is a continuous estimate, not a category - Countries without an ESS estimate stay `lightgrey` because of the `full_join` + `filter(!is.na(Happy_mean))` pattern - Labels use `iso_a3` (from the `World` shapefile) rather than ESS's own 2-letter `cntry` codes, since the two don't share a common code column after the join - `ess_des` (built from `ess_der` in the ESS intro) is reused here ::: ## Likert chart: weighted response distribution by country A map only shows the mean. A Likert-style stacked bar shows the full weighted distribution of raw 0–10 responses within each country. ## Step 1: Normalizing data ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} happy_dist_country <- ess_des |> filter(!is.na(Happy)) |> mutate( Happy_factor = factor( Happy, levels = 0:10, labels = c( "0 - Extremely unhappy", 1:9, "10 - Extremely happy" ) ) ) |> group_by(cntry, Country, Happy_factor) |> summarize(n = survey_total(vartype = NULL)) |> # Normalize within country so each country's bar sums to 100% mutate(p = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup() happy_dist_country ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 327 × 5 cntry Country Happy_factor n p 1 AT Austria 0 - Extremely unhappy 2.90 0.00374 2 AT Austria 1 1.99 0.00256 3 AT Austria 2 3.83 0.00493 4 AT Austria 3 10.9 0.0141 5 AT Austria 4 8.62 0.0111 6 AT Austria 5 43.5 0.0560 7 AT Austria 6 43.2 0.0556 8 AT Austria 7 125. 0.161 9 AT Austria 8 251. 0.323 10 AT Austria 9 198. 0.255 # ℹ 317 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: keep only the happiest and least happy countries To keep the chart readable, show only the `n_countries` countries with the highest and lowest weighted mean happiness (8 total, as in the reference chart). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_countries <- 4 top_bottom_countries <- happy_by_country |> slice_max(Happy_mean, n = n_countries) |> bind_rows( happy_by_country |> slice_min(Happy_mean, n = n_countries) ) |> pull(Country) ``` ::: ## Step 3: order countries by mean and plot ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} happy_likert <- happy_dist_country |> left_join(happy_by_country, by = "Country") |> filter(Country %in% top_bottom_countries) |> mutate(Label = fct_reorder(paste(cntry, "-", Country), Happy_mean)) ggplot(happy_likert, aes(y = Label, x = p, fill = Happy_factor)) + # reverse = TRUE keeps "0 - Extremely unhappy" on the left and # "10 - Extremely happy" on the right, matching the legend order geom_col(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE)) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, name = NULL) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + labs( title = "How happy are you?", subtitle = glue::glue("Top and bottom {n_countries} countries by weighted mean"), x = NULL, y = NULL ) + theme_light() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/happy-likert-plot-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - `survey_total(vartype = NULL)` gives a weighted count per `Country` x `Happy_factor` cell without standard errors, which is all that's needed here since the plot shows a descriptive distribution, not an inferential estimate - Dividing by `sum(n)` within each country (via `group_by(cntry, Country, Happy_factor)` peeling the last group in `summarize()`) turns weighted counts into within-country proportions - `slice_max()`/`slice_min()` on `happy_by_country` pick the `n_countries` happiest and least happy countries; adjust `n_countries` to show more or fewer - `fct_reorder()` sorts the remaining countries by `Happy_mean` so the happiest lands at the top of the plot, matching the ordering convention from the reference chart - `scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1)` gives a diverging blue-to-red palette across the 11 response categories - `position_fill(reverse = TRUE)` is needed because `geom_col()`'s default stacking order would otherwise put "0 - Extremely unhappy" on the right ::: # Your turn # Closing ## References --- nocite: | @* ---

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
